content: Social determinants of health (SDOH) are defined as the conditions in which individuals are born, grow, live, work, and age, as well as the systems established to address illness. These conditions, collectively referred to as social determinants of health, have been acknowledged by various health organizations, including the Public Health Agency of Canada and the World Health Organization, as having a profound impact on both collective and individual well-being. Key factors influencing SDOH include health literacy, employment and working conditions, social environments, physical environments, personal health practices and coping skills, healthy child development, biology and genetic endowment, access to health services, gender, and culture. Disparities in these determinants can significantly affect health outcomes and even influence hospital rankings. The concept of SDOH emerged from research efforts aimed at identifying the specific exposures that lead members of different socioeconomic groups to experience varying levels of health and illness. While it has long been recognized that individuals in different socioeconomic strata experience disparate health outcomes, the precise mechanisms and factors contributing to these disparities required further investigation. Recent analyses and findings on SDOH emphasize the importance of factors beyond biomedical and behavioral risks, such as income and social status. Eleven key social determinants of health have been identified: Aboriginal status, early life experiences, education, employment and working conditions, food security, access to healthcare services, housing, income and its distribution, social safety nets, social exclusion, and unemployment and employment security. A critical emerging issue in the study of SDOH is whether analyses of these determinants are depoliticized. A depoliticized approach fails to consider that the quality of social determinants of health to which citizens are exposed is shaped by public policies created by governments. These governments, in turn, are influenced by political parties that come to power with specific ideological beliefs about the nature of society and the role of government. Analyses that acknowledge the role of politics highlight the importance of having social democratic political parties in power. Countries with a history of prolonged social democratic influence, such as Norway, Finland, Sweden, and Denmark, have implemented government policies that align closely with SDOH principles. In contrast, nations like the USA and Canada, which are predominantly governed by liberal and neo-liberal parties, have shown less alignment with these principles. The work of researchers such as David Coburn, Dennis Raphael, Toba Bryant, Clare Bambra, Richard Hofrichter, Carles Muntaner, and Vicente Navarro has been particularly focused on these issues. An important development in this field has been the establishment of the Social Determinants of Health Listserv at York University. This platform, with over 1,200 members, includes representatives from every state and provincial health authority in the USA, Canada, and Australia, as well as researchers, advocates, and concerned citizens from around the world. Despite these advancements and the growing body of evidence highlighting the critical role of living conditions in health outcomes, public health practice, government policies, and media attention in North America remain predominantly focused on promoting healthy lifestyles and healthy choices. Dennis Raphael at York University has extensively explored the reasons behind this persistent focus, shedding light on the challenges of shifting attention toward addressing the broader social determinants of health.
